claims.evidence: NHS 111 Wales lists memory loss, difficulty concentrating, trouble with familiar daily tasks, struggling to FIND WORDS, confusion about time and place, mood changes. 'Follow conversations' not in retrieved text.
claims.newSentence: NHS pages list memory loss, difficulty concentrating, trouble with familiar daily tasks, difficulty finding words, confusion about time and place, and mood changes as common early symptoms.

claims.evidence: NHS guidance: memory can be affected by stress, tiredness, certain illnesses and medicines; talk to a GP if increasingly forgetful, particularly over 65.
Retrieved NICE text did not state history/physical exam/urine tests. NHS pages say the GP asks about symptoms, examines, and organises blood tests to rule out other causes; urine tests not stated.
claims.newSentence: A GP typically asks about symptoms, carries out an examination and arranges blood tests to look for other causes of memory problems.

claims.evidence: NG97: dementia suspected after reversible causes investigated; referral to a specialist dementia diagnostic service if still suspected.
'Some time before a diagnosis' not found in retrieved text; duplicates c06/c01.
Duplicate of c01 and carries the same unsupported 'follow conversations' detail.
'Often mild and progress very gradually' supported (NHS 111 Wales); 'family and friends may not notice or take them seriously' not found.
claims.newSentence: Early symptoms are often mild and tend to progress very gradually.

claims.evidence: Well-established general fact; not retrieved verbatim in this pass.
NHS guidance: memory can be affected by stress, tiredness, certain illnesses and medicines.
NHS guidance: talk to a GP if someone is becoming increasingly forgetful, particularly over 65.

Retrieved NG97 text only says informant history may be supplemented with structured tools (IQCODE, FAQ); the 'cognitive, behavioural and psychological symptoms and effect on daily life' wording was not found.
claims.newSentence: NICE says a history from someone who knows the person well can be supplemented with a structured tool such as the IQCODE.

claims.evidence: NHS pages mention blood tests to rule out other causes; physical examination and urine tests as NICE recommendations were not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says a GP may arrange blood tests to rule out other causes of memory problems.

claims.evidence: NG97: use a validated brief structured cognitive instrument (e.g. 10-CS, 6CIT) if dementia still suspected; do not rule out dementia solely because of a normal score.
NHS: cognitive tests cannot diagnose dementia alone; diagnosis builds up in stages from several assessments and tests, no single test.
Retrieved text: cognitive tests usually start with a GP; specialist may order CT/MRI; scans also check for other problems. 'Once simpler tests have ruled out other problems' not stated.
claims.newSentence: Memory and thinking tests usually start with a GP, and a specialist may later arrange brain scans such as a CT or MRI scan.

claims.evidence: NG97 text retrieved lists reversible causes (delirium, depression, sensory impairment, anticholinergic medicines) and referral to a specialist dementia diagnostic service; 'memory clinic or community old age psychiatry service' wording not seen.
claims.newSentence: NICE says dementia should be suspected after reversible causes such as delirium, depression, sensory impairment or the effects of some medicines have been looked into, and referral to a specialist dementia diagnostic service applies if it is still suspected.

claims.evidence: NG97: initial specialist assessment includes an appropriate neurological examination and cognitive testing; subtype diagnosed once decline confirmed and reversible causes ruled out.
Leeds and York: first assessment face to face, up to 90 minutes; Berkshire about 1-2 hours; services encourage bringing someone who knows the person well.
Specialist nurse follow-up and 'give yourself time to adjust' not found in retrieved text; also contains a second-person command.
NG97: if not possible to tell whether delirium, dementia or delirium superimposed on dementia, treat for delirium first.

NHS pages (SLaM, NHS 111 Wales) say sudden confusion should lead to A&E or 999 because causes can be life threatening. 111/GP route only appeared in one hospital trust leaflet for post-discharge delirium. 'NHS 111 or a GP is the usual route' could delay urgent care; 'often linked to illness' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Delirium is a sudden state of confusion; NHS pages advise calling 999 or going to A&E for sudden confusion, because some causes can be life threatening and need prompt assessment.

notes: Search summaries blended pages; several NHS statements were attributed to NHS 111 Wales or NHS trust pages rather than nhs.uk pages directly, and nhs.uk symptom text was not returned verbatim (so 'follow conversations' could not be confirmed). NG97 recommendation text was seen only as fragments. c08 is classed textbook but could be checked against the NHS types-of-dementia page. 7 of 8 searches used.
